full_text:
Interviewer:	I’ll give you a bit of background about the research then. We’re interviewing women from across the different engineering disciplines, in their 2nd year. We’re interviewing mainly people who are going on their placement, about their expectations of the placement and also things like why they decided to do engineering in the first place and their course experiences so far. What we’re trying to do is increase women’s retention in the industry, because there’s quite a lot of research now that says that women are going into engineering but they tend to leave after a while. So we’re seeing if there’s any particular reasons why that might be happening and so at the end of the project we’re going to put together a practical guidance document to give to the Engineering Council, to hopefully improve the situation for women in the industry. So I’ll start off just by asking you a few background questions and some stuff about your course. You are doing mechanical engineering, aren’t you?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	What ‘A’ levels did you do?

Subject:	I did maths, I did further maths as an ‘AS’, and chemistry and physics.

Interviewer:	OK, and what type of school did you go to?

Subject:	It was just a normal (?) school – I stayed on a did ‘A’ levels in sixth form.

Interviewer:	Yeah, it wasn’t like an all girls’ school or anything?

Subject:	No, just a normal.

Interviewer:	Ok, have you got any previous experience in the industry?

Subject:	Erm, no not really.

Interviewer:	OK. What do your parents do? Are either of them engineers at all?

Subject:	No they’re not. My mum trained to be an accountant and she now sort of does dad’s book work, he’s a self-employed painter and decorator.

Interviewer:	Right, OK. When and why then do you think that you decided to study engineering?

Subject:	I don’t really know what it was to make me actually do engineering. I think my grades sort of geared me towards doing those ‘A’ levels, and then having chosen them it seemed the logical step. I knew I didn’t want to do erm maths, as a degree subject. I thought it narrowed it down a bit too much, engineering was quite broad (yeah) and sort of where my strengths lie, so that was why I chose the subject.

Interviewer:	So combining all those subjects then that you chose at ‘A’ levels.

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	So were there were any other influences on your decision, like careers advice, or were your family supportive?

Subject:	They were supportive but it was really left to my decision. I sort of got the books out and chose what course I wanted to do. I did sort of think about joining the Navy, which erm may have sort of influenced it because it was more what did I want to do in the Navy? And I wanted to be an engineer. Erm, but that was sort of more before I chose my ‘A’ levels, really.

Interviewer:	OK, did you do much career research into what engineering was about?

Subject:	Not really, no.

Interviewer:	OK, what is it, do you think, that appeals to you about engineering?

Subject:	Erm, I don’t know if it’s one particular thing. It’s certainly the kind of works – the mathematical side of it and sort of seeing how things work and how you can improve them and everything and sort of how my mind’s always worked. So I suppose it was that kind of thing attracted me to it.

Interviewer:	OK, did you ever consider studying any of the other different types of engineering like civil engineering or aeronautical engineering or anything like that?

Subject:	No, not really it was sort of mechanical, through and through, that I wanted to do.

Interviewer:	Yeah, OK, why do you think that was?

Subject:	I really don’t know. Erm, I suppose I considered that it was possibly the broadest of all of them and I thought sort of civil was narrow, you’d only use it one way, aeronautical perhaps – when I sort of first looked at the brochure, just seemed that bit harder and again, you sort of narrowed yourself that way.

Interviewer:	OK, did you know any engineers to talk to?

Subject:	Erm, my uncle, who I’m not sort of particularly close to. Erm but he’s an engineer – I couldn’t actually tell you what sort of engineering he does but he was always sort of saying oh engineering, it’s a good thing to do. Erm, I didn’t really know anyone my age or anything that was going into it.

Interviewer:	Do you think it is just the subjects that you did, that meant it was a natural progression. Do you think if you’d have done other subjects you’d have known what engineering involved?

Subject:	No, because although I didn’t really research it, I knew what engineering was and I knew pretty much what to expect, sort of once I got to university and things. And – but yeah, I suppose it was the subjects that sort of influenced that progression.

Interviewer:	OK, did you always know you wanted to do a sandwich course?

Subject:	No, I didn’t actually. When I first came to Uni, I wasn’t interested at all. Then basically, the more I heard about it the more interested I got.

Interviewer:	OK, we’ll come back to that a bit later on. How did you decide to come to [this] University then?

Subject:	Erm, basically I looked at [university 2] and [this university]. My 2 choices – [this university] was my second choice because [university 2’s] grades were much higher, which I didn’t make. Erm, and it was really just between those 2. I knew that both [this university] and [university 2] were really renowned for their engineering. [university 2] still has the links more with the Navy, than [this university] ever did. So that’s pretty much how I chose.

Interviewer:	OK did you realise that engineering was so male dominated when that’s what you decided to do?

Subject:	Yeah. 

Interviewer:	Did it ever bother you at all?

Subject:	No. 

Interviewer:	OK. Do you think that more women should be encouraged to do engineering?

Subject:	I don’t really know if you can actually encourage people to do something they’re not interested in. I mean, I suppose yeah, there’s some people that wouldn’t necessarily know what engineering was (yeah). But still sort of thinking back to when I did my ‘A’ levels, there were a fair few girls did maths but none of them were interested in engineering. And at that stage they must have known as much as I knew about engineering, so. Yeah, I mean it would be a good thing to have more women in it, but I don’t know quite how you would encourage them in it.

Interviewer:	OK, so do you think maybe, it’s not necessarily about encouraging women to do engineering but maybe at a younger age, giving women the opportunity to know what engineering is?

Subject:	Yeah, because I suppose really right through, from when you did your woodwork projects that at sort of lower school or whatever, it was always women – oh they don’t do that, kind of thing. So perhaps, if it was done yeah – at a younger age – sort of integrated more.

Interviewer:	OK, What characteristics do you think make a good engineer?

Subject:	Ooh, I don’t know. It depends what kind of field you want to go into, I think. I mean some people are sort of really good at coming up with a novel design, whereas others are better at changing what’s already there. Erm, I think you need to have fresh ideas and be able to be quite good at problem solving and team work as well. From what I’ve seen it tends to be mostly, you know, big projects that you’d work together on.

Interviewer:	Ok. Do you think that any of those characteristics are either more male characteristics or more female characteristics?

Subject:	Hmm, till I came to Uni, I would have said that design was more female orientated but I suppose with the fact that it is mostly male on the course, they all seem pretty good at it, so.

Interviewer:	OK Do you think that there are any advantages and disadvantages to being a woman engineer?

Subject:	Erm, I certainly haven’t found it at Uni. I mean there’s obviously always the jokes of oh, the woman, you know, don’t let her touch anything or whatever. But, when it really comes down to it, if you’re working in a group, I think the men tend to be more helpful because you’re female (yeah). So I suppose yeah, it works both ways. I mean you get the disadvantages of the little comments but the advantage is that they actually do help when it comes down to them.

Interviewer:	How do you deal with like getting little comments all the time?

Subject:	I think to be honest, if you’ve chosen to do engineering as a woman, knowing that it’s male dominated, and you’ve got to pretty much the end of your second year, you sort of know what to expect and I wouldn’t really say it’s anything – it’s more sort of banter between people, which I’ve never really had a problem with.

Interviewer:	OK. Has the course been what you expected it to be?

Subject:	Erm, yeah I suppose so.

Interviewer:	OK, are there as many females on the course as you expected there to be?

Subject:	Erm, yeah I’d say there was about what I expected.

Interviewer:	OK. What do you think have been the best and the worst things about the course so far?

Subject:	Oh gosh. Erm, I think probably the worst so far has been a particular group project which has basically run across the whole of this year and you didn’t get to pick the groups you were in, and that was really difficult. I think that’s more like a personal experience as opposed to how everyone found it. The best thing – I’d say that there’s always the support there and the lecturers are really good at – if you’ve got a problem, you can always go and find them and get help. Yeah, that’s probably the best thing.

Interviewer:	OK. Are you pleased that you chose this course then?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	OK. Have you been taught by any female lecturers?

Subject:	Er, yeah – yeah, we were, last semester.

Interviewer:	OK, did you find it encouraging or would you find it more encouraging to have more female lecturers?

Subject:	Er, I don’t really see it makes a difference, to be honest.

Interviewer:	OK. Have you noticed whether the female lecturer has got a different style of teaching to the males, or whether they taught different types of subject at all?

Subject:	Not really, no.

Interviewer:	OK. Do you think that the female lecturers treat you the same as the male lecturers?

Subject:	Erm, it’s kind of hard to say really because the lecturer we had, last semester was – she was actually pregnant so she was ill most of the time and I suppose if you’re actually going to judge it against the others, then in all fairness, and I suppose a lot of the blokes would say this as well, in that ‘cos she was pregnant, it was kind of interrupted our learning, and that’s kind of negative against women in engineering I suppose, so.

Interviewer:	Do you think that affected how any of the lads on your course perceived women in engineering?

Subject:	Erm, not really. I think they were quite good in sort of not seeing it as women in general, but it ‘s quite hard to comment on female lecturers because of that.

Interviewer:	Yeah, she wasn’t a very good example.

Subject:	No, one experience I wouldn’t say is particularly general.

Interviewer:	OK, have you got a personal tutor?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	Are they male or female?

Subject:	They’re male.

Interviewer:	And do you find them approachable?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	Would you rather have a female personal tutor?

Subject:	I don’t see it makes any difference.

Interviewer:	OK. Is there anything or anyone that you’d say has been the biggest influence on you since you started the course?

Subject:	No, not really. There’s no sort of particular thing.

Interviewer:	OK, going back to the group work then, do you have to do quite a lot of group work?

Subject:	Erm, I wouldn’t say it’s a lot. I mean this project, probably seems more because I had a bad experience with it, but in terms of like actual modules, then no, not really. Quite often your course work is done in groups but again, you’ve still got the individual twists on it.

Interviewer:	What has happened in this particular project then?

Subject:	Erm, basically the group that I was part of – erm although I think probably, because it’s only a group of 4, I’d say probably at least 2 out of the other 3 members have got the potential, but really didn’t apply it and everything was always left until the last minute. And obviously if work – it’s supposed to be split 4 ways, 1 person can’t feasibly do it all. Erm, but then I think, like the people in question, they’re other grades in other subjects kind of reflect that anyway, so it’s sort of the level and what they want to achieve from being at uni, I think’s kind of apparent.

Interviewer:	OK, are they male or female people?

Subject:	All male actually.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that men and women bring different characteristics to group work?

Subject:	Erm, yeah, I think from that experience I found that generally the blokes are really laid back, didn’t really care that it wasn’t done till the day before, whereas I consider myself to be a bit more organised and like things structured more, which I think is probably sort of male/female traits.

Interviewer:	Yeah. OK. Do you think there are any advantages of doing group work?

Subject:	Erm, yeah, I think so. I mean obviously you get to see other people’s perceptions on things. And I think it’s quite useful for them dividing the work up, because then you don’t end up doing something – if you find a really good rapport, you can sort of split it to where people’s strengths are.

Interviewer:	Do you think what you’ve learned from group work will benefit you when you go into work as well?

Subject:	I think so, yeah.

Interviewer:	In what way?

Subject:	Everything – sort of basically, I think I know what my strengths are from doing that project, and I’ll be able to sort of take those and know I’m confident in going off and doing say report writing or something. Erm, and I think also, I’ve probably learnt you know how to tolerate problems, because people aren’t always going to pull the same, so that’ll be a help.

Interviewer:	OK, are there any particular aspects of teaching or advice that you think will help you on your placement?

Subject:	Not really. We haven’t really been told that much as to sort of what to expect from the placement – so. The only sort of thing I’ve got is from my actual placement that’s organised what will happen then. What they sort of do and because it’s quite a recognised company, And I think, students obviously like the placement and it works well and so I think I’ve got quite high expectations from that side of it.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that the university should do more to help prepare you?

Subject:	Erm, not really. I mean you don’t have to do the placement anyway – it’s obviously an option. I think the people that have chosen it are wanting to do it for various different reasons but mainly because they want to apply engineering. Erm, and obviously it’s really difficult for them to be able to tell you anyway, ‘cos every placement’s different, so. I mean really you’ve got to know that you’re going to work and you’re gonna be applying some of the stuff you’ve learnt. There’s not really anything else the uni could tell you.

Interviewer:	Do you think that you’ll use a lot of the technical stuff that you’ve learnt on the course?

Subject:	No, I wouldn’t expect so.

Interviewer:	Do you think the main thing you’ll take with you is more the generic skills like your communication skills and group work and things?

Subject:	I’d have said certainly, in the year, the fact that you haven’t finished your degree – you know they’re gonna give you, not necessarily easier but sort of things that are more applicable and – but I think because of the amount of skills that you’ve learnt, in the time at uni, it’s so varied that you’re probably only gonna use – I don’t know – maybe 25% of it., in particular subjects, which is applicable to your engineering – but in what you do use, you’ll develop that far further than you could ever do in a lecture.

Interviewer:	OK, why did you want to go on placement?

Subject:	Erm, it’s kind of hard really because I didn’t want to do it at first and then as the information started coming through, I changed to being on a DIS course, so I had the option. Erm, I basically looked at the fact that you get an extra qualification out of it, but hopefully it’ll improve your grade at the end of it. The skills, obviously that we do take there and use, you’re gonna use so much further than you could learn in a lecture, so hopefully I’ll actually sort of understand applying it rather than well here’s another example, here’s another exam paper. Erm, and I think that side of it, and the fact that I would then be able to come back fresh, you know, finish my degree and then hopefully go and sort of find a job which my placement will sort of assist me in.

Interviewer:	Do you think that when you come back to your final year you will use what you’ve learnt on the placement, as well?

Subject:	I’d have said there’s more a chance of using it in your final year – certainly for final year projects and everything. So what skills you’ve developed on it, will be much sort of easier to choose a project that sort of fits, I would have thought.

Interviewer:	OK, why, when you first started did you think that you didn’t want to do the placement?

Subject:	Erm, well when I first came to uni, it just seemed like an extra year and although I was aware that you got a qualification, I didn’t quite realise that the implications of that putting you so much more ahead of people that have just done the straight course. But I just sort of considered, oh it’s an extra year I don’t sort of want to spend any longer than I have to, getting the qualification, but now I’m sort of seeing it in a different light.

Interviewer:	OK, has anyone discouraged you from going on placement?

Subject:	No

Interviewer:	It’s all been quite positive?

Subject:	Yeah I think so. I haven’t spoken to that many people that have been on placements, but everyone’s sort of said you know it’s a good year out and then you come back sort of fresh to do your degree at the end.

Interviewer:	Yeah, did you say you know where you’re going?

Subject:	Yeah

Interviewer:	And what company is it that you’re going to go to?

Subject:	It’s erm [company].

Interviewer:	OK. What is it that attracted you to them particularly?

Subject:	Erm, I think my main strengths are sort of re-designing things and sort of problem solving, which the job basically will be doing. It will be sort improving what they’ve already got, overcoming problems that they’ve got. Erm, and the fact that they take on a lot of students each year, it’s quite sort of a well known placement and it seems – when I went over for the assessment day, everything was sort of geared towards you. You have loads of opportunities, there were sponsorship opportunities, there was final year project opportunities and just sort of the general camaraderie between everyone – it just seemed like a really good place to go for a year.

Interviewer:	Yeah, and will there be other students doing their placement while you’re there?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	Do you think that that’ll be good?

Subject:	Yeah I do. Originally I started looking at much smaller companies at home, but looking at it in a different light, I think going there and being with other students, that you’re all in the same position and plus [company] as well, will know what we’re capable of, because they’ve taken students before.

Interviewer:	OK, you said you looked at like the sponsorship and things like that … Did you look at the location, or pay and training opportunities?

Subject:	Not so much the location erm ‘cos it’s quite an expensive area, so I suppose if I’d have had anywhere to choose from probably not there.

Interviewer:	Where are they located?

Subject:	Er [town]

Interviewer:	OK

Subject:	The pay wasn’t really an issue actually, because they put it up after I’d applied, so it wasn’t sort of the main incentive. (yeah) The opportunities, once you were there, to be able to erm get trained in all sorts of different things – they do erm like computer learning and you have to be at your desk between certain hours anyway, and if you haven’t got work to do, while you’re at your desk because you’ve got something else on-going, you can actually do these tests, like free your own time, whilst you’re being paid at your desk.

Interviewer:	Oh, that sounds quite good.

Subject:	Seemed like a real bonus. So it can be anything from sort of designing a web page to learning how to use Excel or whatever you choose to do.

Interviewer:	OK, did you apply to any other companies?

Subject:	Erm, I didn’t apply as such to other companies, I more sort of approached them to see if they were interested at all, which most of them sort of weren’t big enough to take a student. Erm, and then I applied to [company] in [town], erm then I went for an interview there. But that seemed actually – quite a good point – it seemed like a really male orientated job and when I got there they were sort of quite shocked to sort of see a female, even to the point where the female toilets were locked and things like that. Erm, it was a lot of sort of hands on welding work and everything.

Interviewer:	What was that company called again?

Subject:	 [Company], so it’s an oil field company and it’s a research position and I basically got there and I was quite shocked actually ‘cos it just seemed like you were going to be sort of a dogsbody, just welding loads of metal and taking the same reading like the same – every day for sort of like a whole year. Erm, and basically the feedback that I got from them was oh you were really good on the day, you know you showed yourself well and everything, but unfortunately we can’t offer you the position and it basically sort of seems like they were looking for a male for the position. And the guy that’s currently on placement, who you’d be taking over from, was sort of really shocked to be showing round a female and kept on sort of oooh, female in engineering and stuff, so…

Interviewer:	So was you quite pleased that you didn’t get that placement then?

Subject:	Yeah, I actually didn’t want it after I’d been there and seen it, I was really quite sort of shocked that companies were still like that, because I didn’t think they were at all.

Interviewer:	OK, did you much research into all of the companies you applied to?

Subject:	Erm, well I thought I had but that was quite a shock when I got there so – [company] I definitely researched into. They sent through information packs and website addresses and everything. But that was actually an assessment, they were kind of expecting you to know a bit about them.

Interviewer:	OK. How involved have the university been in helping you find a placement?

Subject:	Erm, [placement coordinator] in particular was really quite helpful. I spoke to her a couple of times about trying to find a placement that wasn’t what was being sent through. Erm, and she gave me sort of directories to look through and everything. Erm, and then er she looked over my CV personally and sort of went through it with me and everything and definitely, them sending through the placements that were available. I mean I’ve only got one other university to compare it to, that does a sandwich course, but this definitely seems to be like they’re actively trying to find you a placement.

Interviewer:	Yeah, are you happy with the level of involvement then? Would you like them to have done anything else?

Subject:	No, I think it’s been really good actually.

Interviewer:	Yeah, OK, you said about the possibility of getting sponsorship with [company], is that like for your final year?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	Would you be interested in doing that?

Subject:	Er, yeah I think I would

Interviewer:	Did you ever consider getting sponsorship from the start of your course? Did you have that opportunity?

Subject:	No. Well, I certainly wasn’t aware of it, and there wasn’t anything that I sort of would be interested in enough to sort of have that commitment of sponsorship.

Interviewer:	If you did get a sponsorship, would you be expected to go and work for them, when you’ve finished?

Subject:	Erm, I don’t know the full ins and outs but from what I understand you’re not actually expected to. I think you er still have to go through the same interview process for a job once you’ve graduated anyway, but they do take a high proportion of their graduates from people that have done placements. I think it’s something like 70% of all their graduates have done a placement with them. Erm, so it appears that the link’s sort of quite good there.

Interviewer:	Do you think that if you enjoy your placement, you would be happy to go and work for them when you finish?

Subject:	Yeah, I don’t see any reason why not. I think if obviously you’re happy with something.

Interviewer:	OK, is there anything else, that you haven’t already mentioned that you’re hoping to get out of the placement?

Subject:	Mm, no I don’t think so.

Interviewer:	What are you most looking forward to and most worried about going on placement?

Subject:	I wouldn’t say there’s anything I’m actually worried about – there’s a few things I’m apprehensive about, such as you know, who you’re gonna live with and sorting that out. And it seems like a relatively short time as well, because from when I finish here, I start there 5 weeks later but then I know other people who have only got a week, so. Erm, I’m quite excited about meeting new people, working with new people – hopefully learning quite a bit from the year. Erm, slightly apprehensive that they’re gonna expect too much but kind of hoping that when you get there, they’ll be able to assess it like.

Interviewer:	OK, how do you think that being at work will differ from being at university?

Subject:	Erm, I suppose it’ll be more structured, it’s gonna be more sort of 9 to 5. I think there’ll probably be a lot less work to do in your own time, which is probably sort of the main factor, and obviously less holiday but …

Interviewer:	Do you think that you’ll get treated differently?

Subject:	I hope so to be honest. I hope that you’re treated more as one of the actual workers as opposed to you’re still a student. Because students still sort of have this whole, oh you don’t have to get up in a morning and you don’t have to do this and you get however many weeks holiday.

Interviewer:	OK, in terms of your career then, what do you see yourself doing in say 5 years time?

Subject:	Erm, I don’t know. I would like to become a Chartered Engineer – it’s sort of what I’m aiming towards. I suppose I’d like to think that I was really happy with Xerox and they were really happy with me and I ended up there, and I’d probably still be there in 5 years, so.

Interviewer:	What about in say 10 years time? 

Subject:	Oh gosh, I don’t know.

Interviewer:	Do you think you’ll have like climbed the career ladder?

Subject:	I’d like to think so. I’m quite ambitious. I’d certainly like to do more than just have an engineering degree and go into basic engineering.

Interviewer:	Do you think if you do progress upwards, have you got in mind now, whether you’d like to follow like a technical route or a managerial route?

Subject:	I don’t really know, to be honest. I haven’t really considered it that far.

Interviewer:	OK, what do you think then would be your ideal career? Would you still like to go on the Navy?

Subject:	No, I’m not sort of particularly interested in the Navy anymore. Erm, I don’t know what I’d say my ideal was – it’s quite a difficult thing to sort of sit here and say now, especially as I’m about to go on placement.

Interviewer:	If there isn’t an actual job that you can say would be your ideal job, what sort of characteristics do you think your ideal job would have?

Subject:	Erm, definitely some kind of design work. Erm, yeah possibly sort of managerial as well and from being able to basically improve on optimising, so I think those would be the main things.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that’s achievable?

Subject:	I hope so.

Interviewer:	Do you think that there’s anything standing between you and achieving it? Or any difficulties you might encounter?

Subject:	No, I can’t think of any.

Interviewer:	OK, that’s fine. Do you think that the career prospects are good in the type of engineering that you want to go into?

Subject:	Erm, yeah – yeah, I think so…

Interviewer:	Ok, are you happy with all the career choices that you’ve made so far? Would you do anything differently?

Subject:	Yeah – no, I don’t think I would to be honest.

Interviewer:	What 5 words would you use to describe the characteristics of the industry?

Subject:	Mm, erm (pause) I’d say it’s probably quite a technical industry to go into (yeah). I’d say generally quite hard working, erm I think you need to be self-motivated, certainly in terms of coming up with designs and everything. That’s got to be from within you, you’ve got to want to do it. Erm, I think the opportunities are there – I’d say it’s quite a diverse field – they’d probably be the words I’d use.

Interviewer:	OK, would you describe it as masculine?

Subject:	Erm, no. I’d say it’s male dominated I wouldn’t say it’s masculine though.

Interviewer:	What do you think the difference is between the two?

Subject:	I think the fact that it’s male dominated is – I think it really does go back to when you were you know, a much younger sort of age, and it’s a case of oh, women don’t do that. But I wouldn’t say it’s masculine. There’s so many roles in engineering that aren’t even necessarily like hands on work, and they certainly don’t have to be performed by a male.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that the situation will improve for women, in the industry?

Subject:	Yeah, I’d say it probably will. I think it’s already started to, so there’s no reason why it shouldn’t and I suppose more women now are becoming far more career minded as opposed to sort of settling down and having a family young.

Interviewer:	Do you think that women are sometimes made to feel like that they have to choose between career and having a family?

Subject:	No, because I know that I want both and I think, even more so now, for a woman to go back to work, after a family, and continue with her career is quite normal.

Interviewer:	Do you think that it might be hard to achieve because you are in a male dominated industry?

Subject:	No, I don’t think so. I mean so many companies now have their equal rights and everything which they have to follow, but certainly from working in groups that you sort of get on a bit better, that the men are more likely to help you anyway.

Interviewer:	OK, that’s everything, thank you very much, it’s all very helpful.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: I’ll give you a bit of background about the research then. We’re interviewing women from across the different engineering disciplines, in their 2nd year. We’re interviewing mainly people who are going on their placement, about their expectations of the placement and also things like why they decided to do engineering in the first place and their course experiences so far. What we’re trying to do is increase women’s retention in the industry, because there’s quite a lot of research now that says that women are going into engineering but they tend to leave after a while. So we’re seeing if there’s any particular reasons why that might be happening and so at the end of the project we’re going to put together a practical guidance document to give to the Engineering Council, to hopefully improve the situation for women in the industry. So I’ll start off just by asking you a few background questions and some stuff about your course. You are doing mechanical engineering, aren’t you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What ‘A’ levels did you do?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I did maths, I did further maths as an ‘AS’, and chemistry and physics.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, and what type of school did you go to?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It was just a normal (?) school – I stayed on a did ‘A’ levels in sixth form.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, it wasn’t like an all girls’ school or anything?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, just a normal.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, have you got any previous experience in the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, no not really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. What do your parents do? Are either of them engineers at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No they’re not. My mum trained to be an accountant and she now sort of does dad’s book work, he’s a self-employed painter and decorator.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Right, OK. When and why then do you think that you decided to study engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t really know what it was to make me actually do engineering. I think my grades sort of geared me towards doing those ‘A’ levels, and then having chosen them it seemed the logical step. I knew I didn’t want to do erm maths, as a degree subject. I thought it narrowed it down a bit too much, engineering was quite broad (yeah) and sort of where my strengths lie, so that was why I chose the subject.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So combining all those subjects then that you chose at ‘A’ levels.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So were there were any other influences on your decision, like careers advice, or were your family supportive?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: They were supportive but it was really left to my decision. I sort of got the books out and chose what course I wanted to do. I did sort of think about joining the Navy, which erm may have sort of influenced it because it was more what did I want to do in the Navy? And I wanted to be an engineer. Erm, but that was sort of more before I chose my ‘A’ levels, really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, did you do much career research into what engineering was about?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not really, no.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what is it, do you think, that appeals to you about engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I don’t know if it’s one particular thing. It’s certainly the kind of works – the mathematical side of it and sort of seeing how things work and how you can improve them and everything and sort of how my mind’s always worked. So I suppose it was that kind of thing attracted me to it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, did you ever consider studying any of the other different types of engineering like civil engineering or aeronautical engineering or anything like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, not really it was sort of mechanical, through and through, that I wanted to do.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, OK, why do you think that was?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I really don’t know. Erm, I suppose I considered that it was possibly the broadest of all of them and I thought sort of civil was narrow, you’d only use it one way, aeronautical perhaps – when I sort of first looked at the brochure, just seemed that bit harder and again, you sort of narrowed yourself that way.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, did you know any engineers to talk to?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, my uncle, who I’m not sort of particularly close to. Erm but he’s an engineer – I couldn’t actually tell you what sort of engineering he does but he was always sort of saying oh engineering, it’s a good thing to do. Erm, I didn’t really know anyone my age or anything that was going into it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it is just the subjects that you did, that meant it was a natural progression. Do you think if you’d have done other subjects you’d have known what engineering involved?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, because although I didn’t really research it, I knew what engineering was and I knew pretty much what to expect, sort of once I got to university and things. And – but yeah, I suppose it was the subjects that sort of influenced that progression.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, did you always know you wanted to do a sandwich course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, I didn’t actually. When I first came to Uni, I wasn’t interested at all. Then basically, the more I heard about it the more interested I got.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, we’ll come back to that a bit later on. How did you decide to come to [this] University then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, basically I looked at [university 2] and [this university]. My 2 choices – [this university] was my second choice because [university 2’s] grades were much higher, which I didn’t make. Erm, and it was really just between those 2. I knew that both [this university] and [university 2] were really renowned for their engineering. [university 2] still has the links more with the Navy, than [this university] ever did. So that’s pretty much how I chose.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK did you realise that engineering was so male dominated when that’s what you decided to do?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did it ever bother you at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Do you think that more women should be encouraged to do engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t really know if you can actually encourage people to do something they’re not interested in. I mean, I suppose yeah, there’s some people that wouldn’t necessarily know what engineering was (yeah). But still sort of thinking back to when I did my ‘A’ levels, there were a fair few girls did maths but none of them were interested in engineering. And at that stage they must have known as much as I knew about engineering, so. Yeah, I mean it would be a good thing to have more women in it, but I don’t know quite how you would encourage them in it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, so do you think maybe, it’s not necessarily about encouraging women to do engineering but maybe at a younger age, giving women the opportunity to know what engineering is?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, because I suppose really right through, from when you did your woodwork projects that at sort of lower school or whatever, it was always women – oh they don’t do that, kind of thing. So perhaps, if it was done yeah – at a younger age – sort of integrated more.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, What characteristics do you think make a good engineer?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Ooh, I don’t know. It depends what kind of field you want to go into, I think. I mean some people are sort of really good at coming up with a novel design, whereas others are better at changing what’s already there. Erm, I think you need to have fresh ideas and be able to be quite good at problem solving and team work as well. From what I’ve seen it tends to be mostly, you know, big projects that you’d work together on.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok. Do you think that any of those characteristics are either more male characteristics or more female characteristics?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm, till I came to Uni, I would have said that design was more female orientated but I suppose with the fact that it is mostly male on the course, they all seem pretty good at it, so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK Do you think that there are any advantages and disadvantages to being a woman engineer?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I certainly haven’t found it at Uni. I mean there’s obviously always the jokes of oh, the woman, you know, don’t let her touch anything or whatever. But, when it really comes down to it, if you’re working in a group, I think the men tend to be more helpful because you’re female (yeah). So I suppose yeah, it works both ways. I mean you get the disadvantages of the little comments but the advantage is that they actually do help when it comes down to them.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How do you deal with like getting little comments all the time?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think to be honest, if you’ve chosen to do engineering as a woman, knowing that it’s male dominated, and you’ve got to pretty much the end of your second year, you sort of know what to expect and I wouldn’t really say it’s anything – it’s more sort of banter between people, which I’ve never really had a problem with.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Has the course been what you expected it to be?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, yeah I suppose so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, are there as many females on the course as you expected there to be?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, yeah I’d say there was about what I expected.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. What do you think have been the best and the worst things about the course so far?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh gosh. Erm, I think probably the worst so far has been a particular group project which has basically run across the whole of this year and you didn’t get to pick the groups you were in, and that was really difficult. I think that’s more like a personal experience as opposed to how everyone found it. The best thing – I’d say that there’s always the support there and the lecturers are really good at – if you’ve got a problem, you can always go and find them and get help. Yeah, that’s probably the best thing.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Are you pleased that you chose this course then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Have you been taught by any female lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, yeah – yeah, we were, last semester.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, did you find it encouraging or would you find it more encouraging to have more female lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, I don’t really see it makes a difference, to be honest.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Have you noticed whether the female lecturer has got a different style of teaching to the males, or whether they taught different types of subject at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not really, no.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Do you think that the female lecturers treat you the same as the male lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, it’s kind of hard to say really because the lecturer we had, last semester was – she was actually pregnant so she was ill most of the time and I suppose if you’re actually going to judge it against the others, then in all fairness, and I suppose a lot of the blokes would say this as well, in that ‘cos she was pregnant, it was kind of interrupted our learning, and that’s kind of negative against women in engineering I suppose, so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that affected how any of the lads on your course perceived women in engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, not really. I think they were quite good in sort of not seeing it as women in general, but it ‘s quite hard to comment on female lecturers because of that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, she wasn’t a very good example.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, one experience I wouldn’t say is particularly general.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, have you got a personal tutor?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are they male or female?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: They’re male.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And do you find them approachable?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you rather have a female personal tutor?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t see it makes any difference.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Is there anything or anyone that you’d say has been the biggest influence on you since you started the course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, not really. There’s no sort of particular thing.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, going back to the group work then, do you have to do quite a lot of group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I wouldn’t say it’s a lot. I mean this project, probably seems more because I had a bad experience with it, but in terms of like actual modules, then no, not really. Quite often your course work is done in groups but again, you’ve still got the individual twists on it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What has happened in this particular project then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, basically the group that I was part of – erm although I think probably, because it’s only a group of 4, I’d say probably at least 2 out of the other 3 members have got the potential, but really didn’t apply it and everything was always left until the last minute. And obviously if work – it’s supposed to be split 4 ways, 1 person can’t feasibly do it all. Erm, but then I think, like the people in question, they’re other grades in other subjects kind of reflect that anyway, so it’s sort of the level and what they want to achieve from being at uni, I think’s kind of apparent.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, are they male or female people?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: All male actually.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that men and women bring different characteristics to group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, yeah, I think from that experience I found that generally the blokes are really laid back, didn’t really care that it wasn’t done till the day before, whereas I consider myself to be a bit more organised and like things structured more, which I think is probably sort of male/female traits.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah. OK. Do you think there are any advantages of doing group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, yeah, I think so. I mean obviously you get to see other people’s perceptions on things. And I think it’s quite useful for them dividing the work up, because then you don’t end up doing something – if you find a really good rapport, you can sort of split it to where people’s strengths are.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think what you’ve learned from group work will benefit you when you go into work as well?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think so, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: In what way?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Everything – sort of basically, I think I know what my strengths are from doing that project, and I’ll be able to sort of take those and know I’m confident in going off and doing say report writing or something. Erm, and I think also, I’ve probably learnt you know how to tolerate problems, because people aren’t always going to pull the same, so that’ll be a help.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, are there any particular aspects of teaching or advice that you think will help you on your placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not really. We haven’t really been told that much as to sort of what to expect from the placement – so. The only sort of thing I’ve got is from my actual placement that’s organised what will happen then. What they sort of do and because it’s quite a recognised company, And I think, students obviously like the placement and it works well and so I think I’ve got quite high expectations from that side of it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that the university should do more to help prepare you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, not really. I mean you don’t have to do the placement anyway – it’s obviously an option. I think the people that have chosen it are wanting to do it for various different reasons but mainly because they want to apply engineering. Erm, and obviously it’s really difficult for them to be able to tell you anyway, ‘cos every placement’s different, so. I mean really you’ve got to know that you’re going to work and you’re gonna be applying some of the stuff you’ve learnt. There’s not really anything else the uni could tell you.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that you’ll use a lot of the technical stuff that you’ve learnt on the course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, I wouldn’t expect so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think the main thing you’ll take with you is more the generic skills like your communication skills and group work and things?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I’d have said certainly, in the year, the fact that you haven’t finished your degree – you know they’re gonna give you, not necessarily easier but sort of things that are more applicable and – but I think because of the amount of skills that you’ve learnt, in the time at uni, it’s so varied that you’re probably only gonna use – I don’t know – maybe 25% of it., in particular subjects, which is applicable to your engineering – but in what you do use, you’ll develop that far further than you could ever do in a lecture.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, why did you want to go on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, it’s kind of hard really because I didn’t want to do it at first and then as the information started coming through, I changed to being on a DIS course, so I had the option. Erm, I basically looked at the fact that you get an extra qualification out of it, but hopefully it’ll improve your grade at the end of it. The skills, obviously that we do take there and use, you’re gonna use so much further than you could learn in a lecture, so hopefully I’ll actually sort of understand applying it rather than well here’s another example, here’s another exam paper. Erm, and I think that side of it, and the fact that I would then be able to come back fresh, you know, finish my degree and then hopefully go and sort of find a job which my placement will sort of assist me in.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that when you come back to your final year you will use what you’ve learnt on the placement, as well?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I’d have said there’s more a chance of using it in your final year – certainly for final year projects and everything. So what skills you’ve developed on it, will be much sort of easier to choose a project that sort of fits, I would have thought.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, why, when you first started did you think that you didn’t want to do the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, well when I first came to uni, it just seemed like an extra year and although I was aware that you got a qualification, I didn’t quite realise that the implications of that putting you so much more ahead of people that have just done the straight course. But I just sort of considered, oh it’s an extra year I don’t sort of want to spend any longer than I have to, getting the qualification, but now I’m sort of seeing it in a different light.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, has anyone discouraged you from going on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: It’s all been quite positive?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah I think so. I haven’t spoken to that many people that have been on placements, but everyone’s sort of said you know it’s a good year out and then you come back sort of fresh to do your degree at the end.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, did you say you know where you’re going?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And what company is it that you’re going to go to?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It’s erm [company].

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. What is it that attracted you to them particularly?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I think my main strengths are sort of re-designing things and sort of problem solving, which the job basically will be doing. It will be sort improving what they’ve already got, overcoming problems that they’ve got. Erm, and the fact that they take on a lot of students each year, it’s quite sort of a well known placement and it seems – when I went over for the assessment day, everything was sort of geared towards you. You have loads of opportunities, there were sponsorship opportunities, there was final year project opportunities and just sort of the general camaraderie between everyone – it just seemed like a really good place to go for a year.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, and will there be other students doing their placement while you’re there?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that that’ll be good?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah I do. Originally I started looking at much smaller companies at home, but looking at it in a different light, I think going there and being with other students, that you’re all in the same position and plus [company] as well, will know what we’re capable of, because they’ve taken students before.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, you said you looked at like the sponsorship and things like that … Did you look at the location, or pay and training opportunities?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not so much the location erm ‘cos it’s quite an expensive area, so I suppose if I’d have had anywhere to choose from probably not there.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Where are they located?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er [town]

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: The pay wasn’t really an issue actually, because they put it up after I’d applied, so it wasn’t sort of the main incentive. (yeah) The opportunities, once you were there, to be able to erm get trained in all sorts of different things – they do erm like computer learning and you have to be at your desk between certain hours anyway, and if you haven’t got work to do, while you’re at your desk because you’ve got something else on-going, you can actually do these tests, like free your own time, whilst you’re being paid at your desk.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Oh, that sounds quite good.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Seemed like a real bonus. So it can be anything from sort of designing a web page to learning how to use Excel or whatever you choose to do.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, did you apply to any other companies?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I didn’t apply as such to other companies, I more sort of approached them to see if they were interested at all, which most of them sort of weren’t big enough to take a student. Erm, and then I applied to [company] in [town], erm then I went for an interview there. But that seemed actually – quite a good point – it seemed like a really male orientated job and when I got there they were sort of quite shocked to sort of see a female, even to the point where the female toilets were locked and things like that. Erm, it was a lot of sort of hands on welding work and everything.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What was that company called again?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: [Company], so it’s an oil field company and it’s a research position and I basically got there and I was quite shocked actually ‘cos it just seemed like you were going to be sort of a dogsbody, just welding loads of metal and taking the same reading like the same – every day for sort of like a whole year. Erm, and basically the feedback that I got from them was oh you were really good on the day, you know you showed yourself well and everything, but unfortunately we can’t offer you the position and it basically sort of seems like they were looking for a male for the position. And the guy that’s currently on placement, who you’d be taking over from, was sort of really shocked to be showing round a female and kept on sort of oooh, female in engineering and stuff, so…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So was you quite pleased that you didn’t get that placement then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I actually didn’t want it after I’d been there and seen it, I was really quite sort of shocked that companies were still like that, because I didn’t think they were at all.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, did you much research into all of the companies you applied to?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, well I thought I had but that was quite a shock when I got there so – [company] I definitely researched into. They sent through information packs and website addresses and everything. But that was actually an assessment, they were kind of expecting you to know a bit about them.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. How involved have the university been in helping you find a placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, [placement coordinator] in particular was really quite helpful. I spoke to her a couple of times about trying to find a placement that wasn’t what was being sent through. Erm, and she gave me sort of directories to look through and everything. Erm, and then er she looked over my CV personally and sort of went through it with me and everything and definitely, them sending through the placements that were available. I mean I’ve only got one other university to compare it to, that does a sandwich course, but this definitely seems to be like they’re actively trying to find you a placement.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, are you happy with the level of involvement then? Would you like them to have done anything else?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, I think it’s been really good actually.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, OK, you said about the possibility of getting sponsorship with [company], is that like for your final year?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you be interested in doing that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, yeah I think I would

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you ever consider getting sponsorship from the start of your course? Did you have that opportunity?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No. Well, I certainly wasn’t aware of it, and there wasn’t anything that I sort of would be interested in enough to sort of have that commitment of sponsorship.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: If you did get a sponsorship, would you be expected to go and work for them, when you’ve finished?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I don’t know the full ins and outs but from what I understand you’re not actually expected to. I think you er still have to go through the same interview process for a job once you’ve graduated anyway, but they do take a high proportion of their graduates from people that have done placements. I think it’s something like 70% of all their graduates have done a placement with them. Erm, so it appears that the link’s sort of quite good there.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that if you enjoy your placement, you would be happy to go and work for them when you finish?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I don’t see any reason why not. I think if obviously you’re happy with something.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, is there anything else, that you haven’t already mentioned that you’re hoping to get out of the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Mm, no I don’t think so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What are you most looking forward to and most worried about going on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I wouldn’t say there’s anything I’m actually worried about – there’s a few things I’m apprehensive about, such as you know, who you’re gonna live with and sorting that out. And it seems like a relatively short time as well, because from when I finish here, I start there 5 weeks later but then I know other people who have only got a week, so. Erm, I’m quite excited about meeting new people, working with new people – hopefully learning quite a bit from the year. Erm, slightly apprehensive that they’re gonna expect too much but kind of hoping that when you get there, they’ll be able to assess it like.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, how do you think that being at work will differ from being at university?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I suppose it’ll be more structured, it’s gonna be more sort of 9 to 5. I think there’ll probably be a lot less work to do in your own time, which is probably sort of the main factor, and obviously less holiday but …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that you’ll get treated differently?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I hope so to be honest. I hope that you’re treated more as one of the actual workers as opposed to you’re still a student. Because students still sort of have this whole, oh you don’t have to get up in a morning and you don’t have to do this and you get however many weeks holiday.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, in terms of your career then, what do you see yourself doing in say 5 years time?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I don’t know. I would like to become a Chartered Engineer – it’s sort of what I’m aiming towards. I suppose I’d like to think that I was really happy with Xerox and they were really happy with me and I ended up there, and I’d probably still be there in 5 years, so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What about in say 10 years time?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh gosh, I don’t know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think you’ll have like climbed the career ladder?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I’d like to think so. I’m quite ambitious. I’d certainly like to do more than just have an engineering degree and go into basic engineering.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think if you do progress upwards, have you got in mind now, whether you’d like to follow like a technical route or a managerial route?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t really know, to be honest. I haven’t really considered it that far.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what do you think then would be your ideal career? Would you still like to go on the Navy?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, I’m not sort of particularly interested in the Navy anymore. Erm, I don’t know what I’d say my ideal was – it’s quite a difficult thing to sort of sit here and say now, especially as I’m about to go on placement.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: If there isn’t an actual job that you can say would be your ideal job, what sort of characteristics do you think your ideal job would have?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, definitely some kind of design work. Erm, yeah possibly sort of managerial as well and from being able to basically improve on optimising, so I think those would be the main things.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that’s achievable?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I hope so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that there’s anything standing between you and achieving it? Or any difficulties you might encounter?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, I can’t think of any.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, that’s fine. Do you think that the career prospects are good in the type of engineering that you want to go into?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, yeah – yeah, I think so…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, are you happy with all the career choices that you’ve made so far? Would you do anything differently?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah – no, I don’t think I would to be honest.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What 5 words would you use to describe the characteristics of the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Mm, erm (pause) I’d say it’s probably quite a technical industry to go into (yeah). I’d say generally quite hard working, erm I think you need to be self-motivated, certainly in terms of coming up with designs and everything. That’s got to be from within you, you’ve got to want to do it. Erm, I think the opportunities are there – I’d say it’s quite a diverse field – they’d probably be the words I’d use.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, would you describe it as masculine?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, no. I’d say it’s male dominated I wouldn’t say it’s masculine though.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What do you think the difference is between the two?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think the fact that it’s male dominated is – I think it really does go back to when you were you know, a much younger sort of age, and it’s a case of oh, women don’t do that. But I wouldn’t say it’s masculine. There’s so many roles in engineering that aren’t even necessarily like hands on work, and they certainly don’t have to be performed by a male.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that the situation will improve for women, in the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I’d say it probably will. I think it’s already started to, so there’s no reason why it shouldn’t and I suppose more women now are becoming far more career minded as opposed to sort of settling down and having a family young.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that women are sometimes made to feel like that they have to choose between career and having a family?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, because I know that I want both and I think, even more so now, for a woman to go back to work, after a family, and continue with her career is quite normal.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that it might be hard to achieve because you are in a male dominated industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, I don’t think so. I mean so many companies now have their equal rights and everything which they have to follow, but certainly from working in groups that you sort of get on a bit better, that the men are more likely to help you anyway.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, that’s everything, thank you very much, it’s all very helpful.
